claim: The Extended model accounts for multiple features of σ70 binding bacterial promoters to predict constitutive gene expression levels from any sequence.
source: Using random mutant libraries, we developed a biophysical model that accounts for multiple features of σ70 binding bacterial promoters to predict constitutive gene expression levels from any sequence.
evidence: The abstract states this as a main finding, supported by the experimental data from random mutant libraries described throughout the manuscript.

claim: 10–20% of random sequences lead to expression.
source: We experimentally and theoretically estimated that 10–20% of random sequences lead to expression and ~80% of non-expressing sequences are one mutation away from a functional promoter.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by computational simulations and experimental measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ~80% of non-expressing sequences are one mutation away from a functional promoter.
source: We experimentally and theoretically estimated that 10–20% of random sequences lead to expression and ~80% of non-expressing sequences are one mutation away from a functional promoter.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4B and experimental validation in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Selection acts against σ70-RNA polymerase binding sites even within inter-genic, promoter-containing regions.
source: The potential for generating expression from random sequences is so pervasive that selection acts against σ70-RNA polymerase binding sites even within inter-genic, promoter-containing regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genome-wide analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The emergence of promoters is not the limiting step in gene regulatory evolution.
source: This pervasiveness of σ70-binding sites implies that emergence of promoters is not the limiting step in gene regulatory evolution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that promoters readily emerge from random sequences, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Promoters evolve more rapidly than previously thought.
source: Ultimately, the inclusion of novel features of promoter function into a mechanistic model enabled not only more accurate predictions of gene expression levels, but also identified that promoters evolve more rapidly than previously thought.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by evolutionary simulations shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Extended model incorporates six essential structural features of bacterial promoters not present in the Standard model.
source: We developed a comprehensive and generalizable thermodynamic model ('Extended model') that expands on the Standard model by accounting for six essential structural features of bacterial promoters that are not present in the Standard model (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: σ70-RNAP can bind the promoter region in multiple configurations that independently and cumulatively contribute to gene expression.
source: (i) The possibility that σ70-RNAP binds the promoter region in multiple configurations that independently and cumulatively contribute to gene expression (Storz, 2014; Belliveau et al., 2018), as commonly observed in transcriptomics studies (Srikumar et al., 2015).
evidence: This structural feature is described in the text and supported by citations to previous studies and experimental validation in Figure 2A.

claim: Spacer length flexibility assigns an energy penalty for changing the distance between –10 and –35 elements away from the optimum.
source: (ii) Spacer length flexibility, assigning an energy penalty for changing the distance between –10 and –35 elements away from the optimum.
evidence: This is described as a structural feature of the Extended model and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Occlusive unproductive binding occurs when the initiation start site excludes a part of the ribosomal binding site resulting in a non-translated transcript.
source: (iii) Occlusive unproductive binding, occurring when the initiation start site excludes a part of the ribosomal binding site (RBS) resulting in a non-translated transcript.
evidence: This is described as a structural feature and experimentally verified in Figure 2B.

claim: Occlusive binding on the reverse complement strand inhibits productive binding at the promoter.
source: (iv) Occlusive binding on the reverse complement strand, which inhibits productive binding at the promoter (Brophy and Voigt, 2016).
evidence: This is described as a structural feature with citation support and experimental testing shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dinucleotide interactions occur between promoter nucleotide residues that are in direct contact with σ70-RNAP.
source: (v) Dinucleotide interactions between promoter nucleotide residues that are in direct contact with σ70-RNAP.
evidence: This is described as a structural feature and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Extended model accounts for clearance rate of RNAP from the promoter.
source: (vi) Clearance rate of RNAP from the promoter.
evidence: This is described as a structural feature and its optimal value is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The UP element was not accounted for in the Extended model because it has an independent role in determining expression.
source: We do not account for the UP element (Ross et al., 1993), as it has an independent role in determining expression (Einav and Phillips, 2019) and was beyond the scope of this study.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation support.

claim: Cumulative binding, occlusive unproductive binding, and occlusive binding on reverse complement were experimentally verified.
source: We experimentally verified features (i), (iii), and (iv), as, unlike feature (ii), they have not been characterized before (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The experimental verification of unproductive binding on the reverse complement was inconclusive.
source: The experimental verification of unproductive binding on the reverse complement was inconclusive – two sets of promoter mutants changed expression in response to increasing strength of binding on the reverse complement, while the other two sets did not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Including occlusive binding on reverse complement led to a significant increase in predictability, especially of the 36N dataset.
source: However, the inclusion of this feature into the Extended model was justified because it led to a significant increase in predictability (especially of the 36N dataset) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The PR mutant library contained >12,000 constitutively expressed random mutants of bacteriophage Lambda PR promoter.
source: Both, the Standard and the Extended model, were fitted by subsampling a library of >12,000 constitutively expressed random mutants of one of the strongest and best characterized promoters, bacteriophage Lambda PR, that controlled the expression of a yfp reporter gene from a small copy number plasmid in E. coli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental library used for model fitting.

claim: In the PR library, each position in the promoter had a 4% chance of containing each of the non-wildtype bases, resulting in a 12% mutation rate per position.
source: In this library, each position in the promoter had a 4% chance of containing each of the non-wildtype bases, resulting in a 12% mutation rate per position.
evidence: This describes the mutagenesis protocol for the PR library.

claim: Sort-seq experiments were used to measure gene expression levels of mutants.
source: Sort-seq experiments were used to measure gene expression levels of mutants (Kinney and McCandlish, 2019): mutants were separated using a cell sorter into four phenotypic bins ('no', 'low', 'medium', and 'high' expression), PCR-tagged according to the sorted bin, and bulk sequenced to obtain the counts of each mutant sequence in the sorted bins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology with citation support.

claim: The library was randomly split into training (60%), validation (20%), and evaluation (20%) subsets.
source: The library was randomly split into three subsets: 'training' (60% of the sequences), used for training model parameters; 'validation' (20%) used for model selection whenever necessary; and 'evaluation' (20%) used exclusively for final evaluation and visualization of model performance.
evidence: This describes the data splitting methodology.

claim: The energy matrix values obtained by fitting the Extended model correlated strongly with those from a previously published energy matrix of σ70-RNAP (r2 = 0.72; p < 0.001).
source: The energy matrix values obtained by fitting the Extended model correlated strongly with those from a previously published energy matrix of σ70-RNAP, but also exhibited some systematic differences (r2 = 0.72; p < 0.001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Kinney et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both the Standard and Extended models reproduced the evaluation subset of the PR mutant library with high accuracy.
source: Both models, which were fitted on the training subset of the PR dataset only, reproduced the evaluation subset of the PR mutant library with high accuracy, with the Extended model significantly improving on the performance of the Standard model (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The Extended model significantly improved on the performance of the Standard model.
source: Both models, which were fitted on the training subset of the PR dataset only, reproduced the evaluation subset of the PR mutant library with high accuracy, with the Extended model significantly improving on the performance of the Standard model (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The energetic cost of altering the length of the spacer between the –10 and –35 DNA binding elements appears to be approximately quadratic for each deviation away from the optimal 17 bp.
source: (i) the energetic cost of altering the length of the spacer between the –10 and –35 DNA binding elements, which appears to be approximately quadratic for each deviation away from the optimal 17 bp (spacer penalties in Figure 1C)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the inferred model parameters and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Extended model identified 11 positions outside the canonical –10 and –35 elements that directly and independently affect σ70-RNAP binding.
source: (ii) more precise definition of the binding footprint of RNAP compared to previous RNAP energy matrices (Kinney et al., 2010), in particular identifying 11 positions outside the canonical –10 and –35 elements that directly and independently affect σ70-RNAP (energy matrix in Figure 1C)
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 1C with citation to previous work.

claim: The inclusion of occlusive unproductive binding of RNAP to the promoter significantly improves predictability.
source: (iii) the role of occlusive unproductive binding of RNAP to the promoter, which reduces overall expression, and whose inclusion into the model significantly improves predictability (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The PL mutant library shares sequence homology to PR.
source: First, we created a library consisting of random mutants of the Lambda PL promoter, which shares sequence homology to PR.
evidence: This describes the relationship between the PR and PL libraries.

claim: The 36N library consists of completely random 36 nucleotides controlling the expression of a gfp reporter gene.
source: Second, in order to determine model performance across the entire unconstrained genotypic landscape, we built a library consisting of completely random 36 nucleotides controlling the expression of a gfp reporter gene ('36N').
evidence: This describes the 36N library construction.

claim: In the 36N library, each of the 36 positions had a 25% chance of being either adenine, cytosine, guanine, or thymine.
source: In other words, each of the 36 positions had a 25% chance of being either adenine, cytosine, guanine, or thymine.
evidence: This describes the randomization protocol for the 36N library.

claim: ~10% of experimentally measured, random 36-bp-long sequences led to measurable expression.
source: Interestingly, ~10% of experimentally measured, random 36-bp-long sequences led to measurable expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The Extended model dramatically improved predictions of gene expression levels from random sequences compared to the Standard model.
source: While the Extended model trained on the PR library only modestly improved predictability of the PR and local cross-predictability (PL) datasets compared to the Standard model, it dramatically improved predictions of gene expression levels from random sequences (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The improved performance of the Extended model indicates that the structural features accounted for are key components of promoter function.
source: This improved performance of the Extended model compared to the traditional view of promoters (the Standard model) indicates that the structural features we accounted for are key components of promoter function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative model performance.

claim: The inclusion of structural features helps overcome one of the major shortcomings of thermodynamic models of gene expression – their low predictability on novel datasets.
source: In fact, their inclusion helps overcome one of the major shortcomings of thermodynamic models of gene expression – their low predictability on novel datasets (Vilar, 2010), which is observed in Standard model's low predictability of the 36N library.
evidence: This is stated with citation support and demonstrated by comparing model performance.

claim: Each of the structural features included in the Extended model significantly improved predictability.
source: Each of the structural features included in the Extended model (Figure 1A) significantly improved predictability (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Accounting for the energy cost of variable spacer length improved expression level predictions the most.
source: The contribution of each structural feature to predictability differed between mutant libraries, but, in general, accounting for the energy cost of variable spacer length improved expression level predictions the most.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Fitting the Extended model on all three libraries led to further improvements in predictability of expression from random sequences.
source: Fitting the Extended model by subsampling all three libraries (>30,000 mutants), instead of just the PR library, led to further improvements in predictability of expression from random sequences (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Extended model fitted on all libraries resulted in r2 ~0.8, which corresponds to a mean error in expression predictions of 2.8-fold, across a 1000-fold expression range.
source: This resulted in r2 ~0.8, which corresponds to a mean error in expression predictions of 2.8-fold, across a 1000-fold expression range.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative result of model performance.

claim: Dinucleotide interactions are moderate contributors to promoter function.
source: Dinucleotide interactions are moderate contributors to promoter function (Otwinowski and Nemenman, 2013; Figure 2D), and appear to be stronger when at least one residue is outside of the canonical –10 and –35 binding sites.
evidence: This is stated with citation support and shown in Figure 2D and Figure 1C.

claim: The Standard model explicitly assumes that only a single binding position of RNAP governs promoter activity.
source: The Standard model explicitly assumes that only a single binding position of RNAP governs promoter activity, which we model by identifying the single strongest binding site present in each random sequence in the 36N library (in contrast to the Extended model, which considers all possible σ70-RNAP binding configurations cumulatively).
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the Standard model.

claim: The low cross-predictability of the Standard model is often attributed to context dependence.
source: Because of this assumption of the Standard model, its low cross-predictability (i.e. its performance on fully random sequences – Figure 3B) is often attributed to context dependence: the poorly understood effect of positions flanking the –10 and –35 elements (Vilar, 2010; Forcier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The ability of RNAP to bind in multiple configurations to the same promoter led to the improved predictability of the Extended compared to the Standard model.
source: In this study, the ability of RNAP to bind in multiple configurations to the same promoter, rather than a single one, led to the improved predictability of the Extended compared to the Standard model (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a key finding and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Extended model explains away the extensive context dependence as a consequence of the promoter structural features that are accounted for.
source: As such, the Extended model explains away the extensive context dependence as a consequence of the promoter structural features that we account for (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the model's improved performance.

claim: The Extended model (r2 = 0.626) outperformed both the Standard model (r2 = 0.535) and the model presented in Johns et al., 2018 (r2 = 0.47) on the Johns et al. library.
source: As expected, the Extended model (r2 = 0.626) outperformed both the Standard model (r2 = 0.535) and the model presented in the paper (r2 = 0.47) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both the Extended (r2 = 0.602) and the Standard (r2 = 0.598) models had high performance on the Hossain et al., 2020 dataset compared to the model presented in the paper (r2 = 0.45).
source: Both the Extended (r2 = 0.602) and the Standard (r2 = 0.598) models had high performance on the dataset compared to the model presented in the paper (r2 = 0.45), indicating that while the conserved consensus –10 and –35 elements drove a bulk of the observed expression variation, we nevertheless extracted significant predictability gains due to the extended RNAP binding footprint (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Extended (r2 = 0.599) slightly outperformed the Standard model (r2 = 0.588) on the Urtecho et al., 2019 dataset.
source: The Extended (r2 = 0.599) slightly outperformed the Standard model (r2 = 0.588), suggesting that the eight background sequences contained different secondary σ70-RNAP binding sites that cumulatively contributed to expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both the Extended and Standard models underperformed the machine learning approach presented in Urtecho et al., 2019 (r2 = 0.955) on that dataset.
source: However, both models underperformed the machine learning approach presented in the paper (r2 = 0.955) as the expression variation from these modular promoters was driven by interactions between components (Urtecho et al., 2019), which were not captured by the Extended model.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support.

claim: The machine learning model developed by Urtecho et al. considers only combinations of a small number of predefined sequence elements, and as such cannot predict expression level from arbitrary sequences.
source: It is important to emphasize, however, that the machine learning model developed by Urtecho et al. considers only combinations of a small number of predefined sequence elements, and as such cannot predict expression level from arbitrary sequences.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the machine learning approach.

claim: The binding energies and the structural promoter features described in this study are important quantitative determinants of promoter function.
source: First, the high performance of the Extended model on most tested datasets without refitting (comparable to the performance on the 36N library of the Extended model trained only on the PR library), combined with its high predictability of expression from random sequences (the 36N library), suggests that the binding energies and the structural promoter features described in this study (Figure 1) are important quantitative determinants of promoter function.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the model's cross-dataset performance.

claim: The Extended model failed to capture the variation arising from the interactions between various promoter features.
source: Second, while these features are sufficient to predict expression levels from many sequences, especially if sequences are random, the Extended model failed to capture the variation arising from the interactions between various promoter features (Urtecho et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the Extended model with citation support.

claim: Approximately 20% of random 115-bp-long sequences are predicted to have measurable expression.
source: Approximately 20% of random 115-bp-long sequences (average inter-genic region length in E. coli) are predicted to have measurable expression, compared to ~8% for the Standard model (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For ~82% of non-expressing random sequences, at least one point mutation could be found that would led to measurable expression.
source: Surprisingly, for ~82% of non-expressing random sequences, at least one point mutation could be found that would led to measurable expression (Figure 4B) – a finding that we verified experimentally (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: More than 1.5% of all possible point mutations converted a random non-expressing sequence into a functional promoter.
source: In total, more than 1.5% of all possible point mutations converted a random non-expressing sequence into a functional promoter (Figure 4C), indicating that promoter sequences readily emerge, as previously suggested based on a limited sample of ~40 sequences (Yona et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C with citation support.

claim: The Extended model predicts, on average, more rapid evolution from a non-expressing sequence toward either weakest measurable expression or strong expression, when compared to the Standard model.
source: The Extended model predicts, on average, more rapid evolution from a non-expressing sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), toward either weakest measurable expression or strong (wildtype PR level) expression, when compared to the Standard model (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The difference in rates of evolution becomes even more pronounced as the mutating sequence gets shorter.
source: The difference in rates of evolution becomes even more pronounced as the mutating sequence gets shorter (simulating stronger constraints due to, for example, existence of other transcription factor binding sites) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increased rate of promoter evolution predicted by the Extended model means that promoters can evolve even more rapidly than expected based on the standard RNAP consensus sequence or the corresponding energy matrix.
source: The increased rate of promoter evolution predicted by the Extended, as compared to the Standard model, means that promoters can evolve even more rapidly than expected based on the standard RNAP consensus sequence or the corresponding energy matrix.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the evolutionary simulation results.

claim: Under certain conditions, the rate of increase in promoter evolution is several orders of magnitude.
source: Under certain conditions, the rate of increase is several orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in evolutionary rate arises from the inclusion of the new structural promoter features, which dramatically enlarges the number of possible productive binding configurations.
source: This increase arises from the inclusion of the new structural promoter features (Figure 1A), which dramatically enlarges the number of possible productive binding configurations – a phenomenon particularly evident at lower expression levels, where cumulative binding across multiple binding sites substantially contributes to overall expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the increased evolutionary rate and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is strong selection against σ70-RNAP binding sites within genes in E. coli.
source: While identifying strong selection against σ70-RNAP binding sites within genes (Yona et al., 2018), surprisingly, we also found evidence of selection against binding sites in inter-genic regions (p < 10–40 across all inter-genic regions).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E with citation support.

claim: There is evidence of selection against σ70-RNAP binding sites in inter-genic regions (p < 10–40 across all inter-genic regions).
source: While identifying strong selection against σ70-RNAP binding sites within genes (Yona et al., 2018), surprisingly, we also found evidence of selection against binding sites in inter-genic regions (p < 10–40 across all inter-genic regions).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Negative selection against σ70-RNAP binding sites was observed even when only the known, experimentally determined σ70 promoters were considered.
source: This negative selection was observed even when only the known, experimentally determined σ70 promoters (obtained from RegulonDB; Salgado et al., 2013) were considered (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), most of which strongly bind σ70-RNAP and hence lead to intermediate and high expression levels (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and Figure 4F with citation support.

claim: There is selection against σ70-RNAP binding sites not only within genes, but also in the inter-genic regions that contain active promoters.
source: Thus, there is selection against σ70-RNAP binding sites not only within genes, but also in the inter-genic regions that contain active promoters.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genome analysis.

claim: Selection against too many binding sites in promoters could have arisen from a direct competition between σ70-RNAP and other transcription factors.
source: This selection against too many binding sites in promoters could have arisen from a direct competition between σ70-RNAP and other transcription factors, and/or in response to the potential, and poorly understood, cost for a promoter to contain multiple weaker (as opposed to fewer stronger) σ70-RNAP binding sites.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative explanation for the observed selection.

claim: We lack a quantitative link between most cellular processes and DNA sequence.
source: Despite limited success, for example, in connecting the effects of mutations on protein or secondary RNA structures (Schuster, 2006; Dill and MacCallum, 2012), we lack a quantitative link between most cellular processes and DNA sequence.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: We lack a way to decode promoters: a code or dictionary that would map promoter sequences into their function – the level of gene expression.
source: Yet, we lack a way to decode promoters: a code or dictionary that would map promoter sequences into their function – the level of gene expression (Kinkhabwala and Guet, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: This mapping is fundamental for understanding gene regulatory network structure and their evolution.
source: This mapping is fundamental for understanding gene regulatory network structure and their evolution (Voordeckers et al., 2015; Lässig et al., 2017), and for engineering synthetic biological systems (Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Accounting for structural features of promoters improved the predictions of gene expression levels from any DNA sequence, by extending the applicability of thermodynamic modeling toward low expression levels and beyond local neighborhoods of known promoters.
source: Moreover, gene expression is a phenotype that captures our intuitive notion of promoter function, enabling simulation of evolutionary scenarios that select for that function – a feat that appears unrealistic for cases where a phenotype has no obvious functional significance. Accounting for structural features of promoters (Figure 1A) improved the predictions of gene expression levels from any DNA sequence, by extending the applicability of thermodynamic modeling toward low expression levels and beyond local neighborhoods of known promoters (Vilar, 2010; Forcier et al., 2018), to capture the entire genotypic space.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The Extended model allowed us to better understand key mechanisms of promoter function, such as the existence of multiple binding sites that cumulatively contribute to expression.
source: The Extended model also allowed us to better understand key mechanisms of promoter function, such as the existence of multiple binding sites that cumulatively contribute to expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Integrating additional mechanisms of RNAP and promoter function into the Extended model could further improve promoter sequence-to-function predictions.
source: Integrating these and other additional mechanisms of RNAP and promoter function (Hawley and McClure, 1983; Roy et al., 1998) into our Extended model could further improve promoter sequence-to-function predictions.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction with citation support.

claim: The thermodynamic framework can be extended to model complex, regulated promoters that bind transcription factors, as long as their biophysical parameters (energy matrices) are known.
source: Furthermore, the thermodynamic framework can be extended to model complex, regulated promoters that bind transcription factors, as long as their biophysical parameters (energy matrices) are known (Bintu et al., 2005; Saiz and Vilar, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The flexibility of σ70-RNAP binding ensures the proximity of any DNA sequence to a constitutive promoter.
source: The flexibility of σ70-RNAP binding ensures the proximity of any DNA sequence to a constitutive promoter (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The flexibility of σ70-RNAP binding permits easier evolutionary tuning of gene expression levels.
source: This permits easier evolutionary tuning of gene expression levels, while also allowing σ70-RNAP to function as a de facto global regulator (Salgado et al., 2013; Igler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Selection can sustain the binding specificity of required transcription factors and reduce crosstalk while maintaining expression.
source: Selection can thus sustain the binding specificity of required transcription factors and reduce crosstalk while maintaining expression (Friedlander et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The ease of evolving constitutive promoters has been experimentally hinted at using a very limited number of mutants.
source: The ease of evolving constitutive promoters, which has been experimentally hinted at using a very limited number of mutants (Wolf et al., 2015; Yona et al., 2018), remained theoretically puzzling (Tuğrul et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Tugrul et al. failed to identify mechanistic or evolutionary factors that would increase the predicted speed of binding site evolution and bring it closer to experimental observations.
source: In fact, Tugrul et al. failed to identify mechanistic or evolutionary factors that would increase the predicted speed of binding site evolution and bring it closer to experimental observations.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work.

claim: Promoters evolve more rapidly than expected based on existing models of protein-DNA interactions.
source: To address this discrepancy, we linked an extended biophysical model of promoter function, inferred directly from large mutant libraries, with a quantitative evolutionary framework to show that promoters indeed evolve more rapidly than expected based on existing models of protein-DNA interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding from the evolutionary simulations.

claim: The increase in the rates of promoter evolution can be orders of magnitude faster in the Extended compared to the Standard model.
source: Strikingly, this increase in the rates of promoter evolution, which can be orders of magnitude faster in the Extended compared to the Standard model, arises from the same promoter features that account for only a 2-to-3-fold increase in the likelihood of random sequences resulting in measurable expression.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the evolutionary simulations.

claim: The potentiation in evolutionary rate likely comes about due to a vast expansion in the number of accessible evolutionary paths that lead from a random initial sequence to the functional promoter, likely created by the flexible spacer.
source: We hypothesize that this potentiation comes about due to a vast expansion in the number of accessible evolutionary paths that lead from a random initial sequence to the functional promoter, likely created by the flexible spacer, which is an interesting question for future research.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: Biophysical models that accurately capture mechanisms of biological function offer a robust method for addressing key questions in biology and evolution.
source: Our study shows how biophysical models that accurately capture mechanisms of biological function offer a robust method for addressing key questions in biology and evolution.
evidence: This is stated as a general conclusion from the study.
